items.item: The hook's own two measurements are not a contest between two different kinds of database; they are the same engine answering two differently sized questions, which is exactly the distinction the predict step is built to isolate before naming pre-aggregation as the actual mechanism.

at.step: Hook: the same query, measured for real: scanning raw rows from scratch versus a table that already holds the answer

items.item: Framing pre-aggregation as a cost shift rather than a cost cut matters because it predicts where the hidden cost reappears: not in the fast read, but in whatever process keeps the materialized table updated, which is exactly what the next reveal's freshness gap measures directly.

at.step: Reveal: pre-aggregation is a cost shift, not a cost cut

items.item: The measured speedup in examples.py is not a one-off artifact of DuckDB specifically; any engine pays roughly the same cost to scan and combine a large raw table versus reading a small precomputed one, which is why the same shape of result shows up across very different real systems.

at.step: Reveal: a materialized serving table, measured

items.item: The freshness gap measured here is a design choice, not a bug: a materialized table could be kept perfectly fresh by refreshing it on every single write, but that would erase the entire cost-shift benefit this topic's earlier reveal named, since the work would again happen on every write.

at.step: Reveal: the freshness gap, measured

items.item: A cube's own storage cost grows with the number of dimension combinations it precomputes, not with the size of the raw data alone, so a cube is a real trade-off against more dimensions, not a free generalization of a single materialized table.

at.step: Reveal: cubes generalize this to many questions at once

items.item: Rollup losing the ability to query individual events is a direct consequence of pre-aggregating at ingestion rather than losing information arbitrarily: once rows with the same dimension values and timestamp are combined into one, the real system no longer has any way to tell which original event contributed what.

at.step: Reveal: a real-time OLAP store's own rollup

items.item: This topic's own three options sit on a real spectrum, not three unrelated choices: a raw warehouse scan is always fresh and never pre-aggregates; a materialized view pre-aggregates on a schedule; a real-time OLAP store pre-aggregates on every single write — each step trading a little more staleness risk for a lot more read-time speed and write-time cost.

This topic establishes which of three real techniques to reach for when serving an aggregate; it says nothing yet about how a consumer reads what a producer already wrote in the first place, which is exactly the gap the next topic closes by turning to queues and logs.

The 'Prove it' step's own correct answer depends on both halves of the trade-off at once, not either alone: a team that only cared about freshness could over-pay for a real-time OLAP store even at low query volume, and a team that only cared about cost could under-provision freshness even when correctness truly needs it.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: Pre-aggregation's own cost-shift idea connects directly back to this chapter's earlier cache material: a cache-aside layer also shifts work (a backing-store read) to the moment a miss happens rather than every request, which is the same underlying trade this topic names for aggregation specifically.
